evidence: Cic. Fam. 5.12.4: ad dēlectātiōnem lēctōris (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The reader of a book. Lewis & Short’s other senses: a slave who read aloud to his master (Quint. 2.5.6, Plin. Ep. 9.17.3), and in the Church a lector (Tert.). The long ē by Lachmann’s law, from lēctus.

phrases.latin: quid ergō possum facere tibi, lēctor Catō, sī nec fābellae tē juvant nec fābulae?
phrases.english: So what can I do for you, my Catonian reader, if neither little stories please you nor big ones?

lector.html: From lēctus, legō: Lachmann’s law; Gellius 9.6.3 on āctitō from āctus.

sources: Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-phaedrus), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
